name: Fermented vegetables
standfirst: Every one of these is a vegetable held under brine, or under its own juice, until lactic bacteria turn it sour — the wild ones that came in on it, or the ones handed over in a starter. What separates them is how the salt gets in, what goes in with it, how cold it is kept and for how long — and whether you stop while it still cracks.
root: Raw or barely scalded vegetable · held under brine or packed tight · lactic bacteria, wild or from a starter

nestings.label: By how the salt goes in

dishes.name: Sauerkraut
dishes.note: No brine is poured in. The salt pulls one out of the cabbage, and the weight holds the cabbage under it — that is the whole trick.

dishes.name: Suan cai
dishes.note: Whole napa heads rather than shreds, held down by a stone and topped up with water, and cold enough that the ferment takes all winter instead of a month. Sauerkraut reached independently.

dishes.name: Ogórki kiszone
dishes.note: The horseradish leaf is not seasoning. Its tannins slow the enzymes that soften the cucumber — the one ingredient here whose job is texture. What it buys is weeks rather than crunch: the cucumber goes soft in the end, only later than it would have.

dishes.name: Kimchi
dishes.note: The only one salted twice over: brined to draw water out, rinsed so it is not inedible, then packed with a seasoning of chilli powder, garlic and salted shrimp that ferments alongside it.

dishes.name: Dongchimi
dishes.note: Not kimchi minus the paste — it is older than chilli in Korea. The liquid is strained off for cold noodle broth.

dishes.name: Pao cai

salt: never touched with an oily hand

dishes.note: The jar has a water moat round its lid: gas escapes, air never gets back in. The old brine is kept going for decades and inoculates each new batch.

dishes.name: Zha cai
dishes.note: The knobbed stem of a mustard plant, not a leaf, grown at Fuling on the Yangtze. It is hung to wilt before any salt goes near it, and pressing it three times is what leaves it crunchy after half a year in the jar.

dishes.name: Nukazuke

salt: buried in a wet rice-bran bed
add: a bran bed kept alive for years

dishes.note: The bed is the dish and the vegetable is a guest — cucumbers go in at night and come out at breakfast, and the nukadoko is fed and stirred forever.

dishes.name: Dưa cải chua
dishes.note: Mustard greens, wilted a few hours so they bend into the jar. The rice water and the sugar are both there to get the bacteria moving before anything else does.

dishes.name: Torshi left
dishes.note: Turnip. The beetroot is one slice and it is there entirely for the colour. The Persian sense of torshi usually means vinegar instead — this is the salt-brine branch.

dishes.name: Şalgam suyu

end: the black carrot does the fermenting
a slice goes back in the glass

dishes.note: The name says turnip, but the black carrot is what ferments and the turnip goes in beside it for aroma. The brine is served cold beside kebab, and a slice of the carrot goes into the glass as it is poured, often with garlic or chilli.

dishes.name: Kanji
dishes.note: Black carrot fermented into a sour drink, set out in the winter sun to keep the jar warm — the same answer Adana arrived at, except that nothing is added to start it. The mustard keeps the competition down and the carrots bring their own bacteria.

dishes.name: Gajar gobhi shalgam achar
dishes.note: The winter pickle: the vegetables are dipped in boiling water and dried in the sun before any salt goes near them. Oil on top does what a brine does elsewhere — seals the surface — and the jaggery gives the bacteria something to eat.

dishes.name: Curtido
dishes.note: Three days, not three weeks, so it is a relish rather than a preserve. The scald is argued over — skip it and the ferment starts faster.

dishes.name: Gundruk
dishes.note: No salt anywhere in it. Bruising the leaves floods the pot with their own juice fast enough that nothing else gets a foothold — then it is sun-dried and keeps for a year.

dishes.name: Gari
dishes.note: Cassava, and the ferment is not for flavour — it breaks down the cyanide that makes the raw root poisonous. Toasting on a hot pan ends it.

notes.title: On salt
notes.body: Salt ferments nothing. It pulls water out of the vegetable into a brine that lactobacillus tolerates and most spoilage organisms do not — it is a doorman, not a cook. Brining and dry-salting are two routes to the same brine: one you mix, the other the cabbage makes. Gundruk and gari dismiss the doorman entirely and rely on speed instead, and on shutting the air out by sealing the pot or pressing the mash dry.

notes.title: On where you stop
notes.body: Crunch is pectin, and pectin is lost to warmth and time rather than to salt. The same jar of cucumbers is a crisp half-sour at three days on the counter and a soft full-sour at three weeks, with nothing added in between. The crunchy column is mostly cold, or quick, or both. The exceptions are zha cai and the turnip in torshi left, both dense stem-and-root rather than leaf, which is why they hold where a cabbage would collapse — which is neither: it is wilted and then pressed three times over until there is too little water left in it to soften.

notes.title: On depth
notes.body: Nothing here sits under anything else. Kimchi is not dongchimi with chilli paste added — dongchimi is older than chilli in Korea, and both descend from the same habit of salting vegetables down for the winter. Sauerkraut and suan cai are one idea arrived at twice by people who never met. Siblings, all of them.
